title: 0. Programming Fundamentals
description: Language-agnostic building blocks tested heavily on Turing Stage 1 MCQ and Andela A1/A3. Variables, memory model, closures, complexity, types, recursion, OOP. Each question carries a real per-question time budget matching the actual test.

0.1 Variables & Memory: Pass by value vs pass by reference (JS/Python: pass by value of reference)
0.2 Functions & Closures: Scope: lexical vs dynamic, block vs function vs module
0.3 Complexity Analysis: Common classes: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2^n), O(n!)
Recurrence relations (T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → O(n log n))
0.7 Conditional & Logic Problem-Solving: if / else if / else / switch expressions
Ternary vs full if — when to use which
Handling edge cases: null, empty, negative, overflow

questions.prompt: In most modern languages (Python, JS, Java), when you write `a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4)`, what does `a` now contain?
questions.explanation: `b = a` copies the REFERENCE, not the value. Both names point to the same underlying list. Mutating through one is visible through the other.

questions.prompt: Which of these types is IMMUTABLE in most languages (Python str, Java String, JS string)?
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable — any 'modification' produces a NEW string. Lists, dicts, and sets are mutable containers.

questions.prompt: Which are TRUE about the STACK memory region? (select all)

options.text: Stores function call frames + local variables
Automatically freed when the function returns
Unbounded — grows as much as you need

questions.explanation: Stack is fast, LIFO, per-thread, and BOUNDED (typically ~1-8 MB) — that's why deep recursion causes StackOverflow. Heap is larger, slower, manually or GC-managed.

questions.prompt: Where does a Java `new Object()` live?

options.text: Object on the heap; the local reference to it on the stack

questions.explanation: Java objects are heap-allocated. The local variable holding the reference lives on the stack. Same model in Python, JS, C#.

questions.prompt: Python, JS, and Java are best described as:

options.text: Pass by value of the reference (aka 'call by sharing')

questions.explanation: The reference is copied (so reassigning the parameter doesn't affect the caller), but both refs point to the same object (so mutation is visible). C++ has true pass-by-reference with `&`.

questions.prompt: In Python, what does this print?
questions.code:
def f(lst):
    lst = [9, 9]

a = [1, 2, 3]
f(a)
print(a)
questions.explanation: Reassigning the parameter inside the function replaces the LOCAL binding. The caller's `a` still points to the original list. Use `lst.clear(); lst.extend([9,9])` or `lst[:] = [9,9]` to mutate.

questions.prompt: Python `is` vs `==`:

options.text: `is` checks object identity (same memory); `==` checks value equality

questions.prompt: Which languages use REFERENCE COUNTING as the PRIMARY GC strategy?
questions.explanation: CPython = refcount + cycle detector fallback. JVM, V8, Go use generational/mark-and-sweep GC. Refcount can't detect cyclic references alone.

questions.prompt: Which are COMMON causes of memory leaks even with a garbage collector? (select all)

options.text: Growing global cache with no eviction

questions.explanation: A leak = reachable object that will never be used again. `const` vs `let` is scope/binding, not leak-related.
`[:]` is a SHALLOW copy — outer list is new but inner lists are shared references. Use `copy.deepcopy(a)` for true independence.

questions.prompt: Python `a = 256; b = 256; a is b` → True. But `a = 257; b = 257; a is b` → False (in CPython). Why?

options.text: CPython interns small integers (-5 to 256) — they share objects. Larger ints are fresh objects.

questions.explanation: Small-int cache is an implementation detail. NEVER use `is` for value comparison — use `==`. Same idea: some strings are interned (`sys.intern`).

questions.prompt: A weak reference:

options.text: Does NOT prevent GC; lets you observe the object without keeping it alive

questions.explanation: Useful for caches: entries evict automatically when no strong references remain. Python `weakref`, JS `WeakMap`/`WeakRef`, Java `WeakReference`.

questions.prompt: Java `Integer` vs `int` — key difference:

options.text: `int` is a primitive on the stack; `Integer` is a heap object wrapper — nullable but slower, boxing/unboxing cost

questions.explanation: Generics require reference types → `List<Integer>` not `List<int>`. Java 21+ Project Valhalla aims to remove this gap.

questions.prompt: Python — what does this print?
questions.code:
def f(x, seen=[]):
    seen.append(x)
    return seen

print(f(1))
print(f(2))
questions.explanation: Mutable default arg is evaluated ONCE at function definition and reused across calls. Fix: `def f(x, seen=None): seen = seen or []`.

questions.prompt: Why does iterating a large 2D array row-by-row often beat column-by-column?

options.text: CPU cache locality — row-major storage means consecutive row elements are contiguous in memory, so cache lines are used efficiently

questions.explanation: C/C++/NumPy default to row-major. Fortran / MATLAB / Julia are column-major. Iterate along the storage direction.

questions.prompt: A local variable is:

options.text: Declared inside a function/block; alive only for that scope's execution

questions.explanation: Locals live on the stack for the duration of the call. They're not visible outside their block or function.

questions.prompt: Lexical scope means:

options.text: Name lookup follows the call stack at runtime
Name lookup follows the WRITTEN nesting of blocks/functions — determined at compile time

questions.explanation: Most modern languages are lexically scoped. Bash, Perl (`local`), and early Lisp used dynamic scope.

questions.prompt: What does this print (Python)?
questions.code:
def make_counter():
    c = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal c
        c += 1
        return c
    return inc

counter = make_counter()
print(counter(), counter(), counter())
questions.explanation: `inc` closes over `c` in the enclosing scope. `nonlocal` lets us REASSIGN it (without nonlocal, Python treats `c += 1` as a local write and errors).

questions.prompt: A closure is:

options.text: A function bundled with references to variables from its enclosing lexical scope

questions.explanation: Closures enable data-hiding + factory functions. Anonymous functions can BE closures but the two concepts are distinct.

questions.prompt: A PURE function must: (select all)

options.text: Return the same output for the same input
Have no side effects (no I/O, no mutation of external state)
Not depend on external mutable state

questions.explanation: Determinism + no side effects. Recursion and async are orthogonal.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a higher-order function?
questions.explanation: HOFs take or return functions. `len` operates on data. `map/filter/reduce` all take a function argument.

questions.prompt: What does this print (Python)?
questions.code:
fns = []
for i in range(3):
    fns.append(lambda: i)
print([f() for f in fns])
questions.explanation: All lambdas close over the same `i`; after the loop `i == 2`. Fix: `lambda i=i: i` to capture the current value as default.

questions.prompt: Which is a side effect?

options.text: Modifying a global variable, writing to a file, or calling print()

questions.explanation: Anything observable beyond returning a value = side effect. Pure functions have none.

questions.prompt: Currying transforms `f(a, b, c)` into:

options.text: f(a)(b)(c) — a chain of single-arg functions

questions.explanation: Currying enables partial application. `add(2)(3)` returns 5 if `add = a => b => a + b`. Common in FP and libraries like Ramda.

questions.prompt: 'Functions are first-class' means:

options.text: They can be assigned to variables, passed as args, returned from other functions

questions.explanation: First-class citizens of the language. Python, JS, Ruby, Scala, Haskell — all first-class. C traditionally works with function POINTERS, close but not identical.

questions.prompt: Partial application:

options.text: Fixes SOME arguments now, leaving the rest for later
Calls the function partway then aborts
Runs the function on a subset of data

questions.explanation: `add5 = partial(add, 5)`; `add5(3) → 8`. Different from currying, though both produce specialised functions.

questions.prompt: What is an IIFE (Immediately-Invoked Function Expression) used for?

options.text: Creating a private scope to avoid polluting the global namespace (classic JS pattern pre-modules)

questions.explanation: `(function(){ var x = 1; })();` — the `var` is trapped in the IIFE's scope. Largely obsolete with ES modules but still seen in library bundlers.

questions.prompt: Referential transparency means:

options.text: You can see the source code
An expression can be replaced with its value without changing program behavior

questions.explanation: Pure functions give referential transparency. Enables aggressive optimizations (memoization, common subexpression elimination) and equational reasoning.

questions.prompt: In JS, arrow functions differ from regular functions in that:

options.text: They inherit `this` from the enclosing lexical scope + lack their own `arguments` object

questions.explanation: Arrows are lexically-`this` bound. That's why they're preferred inside methods that pass callbacks — no need for `.bind(this)`.

questions.prompt: Choosing iteration over recursion is BETTER when: (select all)

options.text: The language doesn't do tail-call optimization
You want the shortest possible code

questions.explanation: Recursion is elegant but each call costs a stack frame. Python has no TCO. Convert to iteration or use an explicit stack for deep structures.

questions.prompt: Big-O notation describes:

options.text: An asymptotic upper bound on growth as input size increases

questions.explanation: Big-O = upper bound (worst case). Big-Θ = tight bound. Big-Ω = lower bound. Constants and lower-order terms dropped.

questions.prompt: Which is O(1)?
questions.explanation: Array-by-index is constant. Hash-map get/set is amortized O(1). Stack push/pop O(1). Linked-list access by index is O(n).

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array of size n is:
questions.explanation: Each step halves the search space → ⌈log₂ n⌉ steps. Requires sorted, random-access data.

questions.prompt: Two nested loops both from 0 to n:
questions.explanation: n × n = n². For sequential (not nested) loops: O(n + n) = O(n).

questions.prompt: For each of n elements, you do a binary search on an m-sized array. Complexity?
questions.explanation: Multiplicative: n outer steps × O(log m) each.

questions.prompt: An algorithm does 3n² + 5n + 100 operations. Its Big-O is:
questions.explanation: Drop constants + lower-order terms → O(n²). Big-O captures asymptotic behavior.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithms are O(n log n) AVERAGE case? (select all)
questions.explanation: Bubble + insertion are O(n²) avg. Quicksort is O(n²) WORST case (bad pivots) but O(n log n) avg. Mergesort + heapsort are O(n log n) worst.

questions.prompt: Python list `append` is O(1) AMORTIZED. What does amortized mean here?

options.text: Sometimes triggers a resize (O(n)), but averaged over many operations the cost per op is O(1)

questions.explanation: Dynamic arrays double capacity on resize → geometric growth → total copying work is O(n) across n appends. Same idea for hash-map growth.

questions.prompt: The space complexity of iteratively summing n integers into one accumulator is:

options.text: O(1) — a single accumulator regardless of n

questions.explanation: Recursive sum would be O(n) space due to call stack. Iterative = O(1) auxiliary.

questions.prompt: T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n) resolves to:
questions.explanation: Merge sort's recurrence. Master Theorem case 2 (a=2, b=2, log_b(a)=1 = exponent of n) → n^{log_b a} × log n = n log n.

questions.prompt: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) resolves to:
questions.explanation: Binary search's recurrence. One recursive call, halving input each time.

questions.prompt: In Big-O, `O(log₂ n)` and `O(log₁₀ n)` are:

options.text: The same — Big-O ignores the log base (they differ by a constant factor)

questions.explanation: log_a n = log_b n / log_b a → constant factor. Big-O drops constants.

questions.prompt: Naive recursive Fibonacci (no memo) has time complexity:
questions.explanation: Actually O(φ^n) where φ ≈ 1.618, but bounded by O(2^n). Memoization brings it to O(n).

questions.prompt: Order from FASTEST-growing to SLOWEST: n log n, log n, n², n, 2^n

options.text: 2^n > n² > n log n > n > log n
n² > 2^n > n log n > n > log n
log n > n > n log n > n² > 2^n
2^n > n log n > n² > n > log n

questions.explanation: Standard hierarchy: constant < log < √n < linear < n log n < quadratic < cubic < exponential < factorial.

questions.prompt: Hash-map lookup is O(1) average but WORST case is:

options.text: O(n) — all keys colliding into one bucket (adversarial input or bad hash)

questions.explanation: Java 8+ HashMap promotes long collision chains to red-black trees → worst becomes O(log n). Adversarial hash attacks are why frameworks now randomize hash seeds.

questions.prompt: Insertion sort's best-case complexity (already sorted input):
questions.explanation: One pass, no swaps. Worst case (reverse sorted) is O(n²).

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS on a balanced binary tree uses what space?

options.text: O(log n) — call stack depth = height

questions.explanation: Balanced tree height = log n. Skewed tree = O(n) call stack, risk of overflow.

questions.prompt: A hash-map trades what for O(1) average lookup?

options.text: Extra memory + unpredictable iteration order + O(n) worst-case collisions

questions.explanation: Data-structure choices are trade-offs. Balanced BSTs give O(log n) lookup + ordered iteration + no adversarial worst.

questions.prompt: Static vs dynamic typing — the key difference is:

options.text: Static: types checked at COMPILE time (Java, Go, TS). Dynamic: types checked at RUNTIME (Python, JS, Ruby).

questions.explanation: Orthogonal to strong/weak. Python is strong + dynamic; JS is weak + dynamic; Haskell is strong + static.

questions.prompt: Strong vs weak typing:

options.text: Strong: implicit conversions are limited (Python: '5' + 5 → TypeError). Weak: many implicit conversions (JS: '5' + 5 → '55').

questions.explanation: Strong typing catches more bugs earlier at runtime. Weak-typed languages need extra care around ==, +, coercion.

questions.prompt: JavaScript — what does this print?
questions.explanation: Left-to-right: `1 + '1'` → string concat → '11'. Then `'11' - 1` → numeric coercion → 10.

questions.prompt: Type inference in languages like Go, Rust, TS means:

options.text: Types are optional and never checked
The compiler derives the type from context (`let x = 5` → x is int)

questions.explanation: You get compile-time safety without annotation clutter. Hindley-Milner (Haskell, ML) infers whole-program types; local inference (Go, TS) infers per-declaration.

questions.prompt: In Java, which is a REFERENCE type?
questions.explanation: Primitives: byte, short, int, long, float, double, boolean, char. Everything else is a reference type (including arrays).

questions.prompt: Which language design ELIMINATES null pointer exceptions by design?
questions.explanation: Sum types (Option/Maybe) or nullable-annotated types force explicit handling. Tony Hoare called null 'the billion-dollar mistake'.

questions.prompt: JavaScript — what does this print?
questions.explanation: `[]` → primitive '' → 0. `false` → 0. So true. `![]` → false → 0. `[]` → 0. So true. `==` coercion is why the community pushes `===`.

questions.prompt: Duck typing means: (select all)

options.text: 'If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck'
Objects are usable if they have the required methods/attributes — no declared interface needed

questions.explanation: Compatibility judged by behavior at use-site rather than declared type. Trade-off: flexibility vs compile-time safety. Python 3 added Protocols for structural typing.

questions.prompt: Autoboxing in Java is:

options.text: Automatic wrap of a primitive in its object type (`int` → `Integer`) and back

questions.explanation: Enables `List<Integer>` to accept `int` literals. Has runtime cost + null-pointer trap on unbox.

questions.prompt: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` in most languages?

options.text: IEEE 754 floats can't exactly represent 0.1 or 0.2 in binary; the sum is 0.30000000000000004

questions.explanation: For money, use decimal types (Python `Decimal`, Java `BigDecimal`, C# `decimal`) or work in cents as integers.

questions.prompt: Every recursive function needs a:

options.text: Base case — the terminating condition that stops recursion

questions.explanation: Without a base case, infinite recursion → StackOverflowError.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
Python's default recursion limit is:
questions.explanation: Python has NO tail-call optimization. Convert deep recursion to iteration or use an explicit stack.

questions.prompt: A tail-recursive function:

options.text: Recurses on the base case first
Makes its recursive call as the very last operation, allowing the compiler (if TCO-capable) to reuse the current stack frame

questions.explanation: Scala, Scheme, Haskell, Erlang do TCO. JS strict mode was supposed to (only Safari implemented). Python + Java don't.

questions.prompt: Memoization speeds up naive Fibonacci from O(2^n) to:

options.text: O(n) — each subproblem computed once, cached

questions.explanation: Trade extra O(n) memory for exponential time savings. Foundation of DP.

questions.prompt: Which of these problems is MOST NATURALLY expressed recursively?
questions.explanation: Recursive structures (trees, nested data) map cleanly to recursive functions. Iterative sum is more efficient.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Mutual recursion. 4 → is_odd(3) → is_even(2) → is_odd(1) → is_even(0) → True.

questions.prompt: To convert a recursive tree traversal to iteration, you typically use:

options.text: A while loop with a global
An explicit stack (or queue for BFS)

questions.explanation: The call stack IS a stack. Making it explicit lets you handle deeper trees without StackOverflow.

questions.prompt: A class is:

options.text: A blueprint / template. Instances are concrete objects created from it

questions.explanation: `Dog` is a class; `my_dog = Dog('Rex')` is an instance. One class → many instances.

questions.prompt: The four pillars of OOP are:
questions.explanation: EIPA. Some lists swap Abstraction for Composition or drop it entirely.

questions.prompt: Encapsulation is:

options.text: Bundling data + methods that operate on it, and restricting direct access to internal state

questions.explanation: Private fields + public methods lets you evolve internals without breaking callers.

questions.prompt: Class `Dog extends Animal`. `Dog` can:

options.text: Access Animal's public/protected members and override any virtual methods

questions.explanation: Inheritance = 'is-a' relationship. Overriding lets Dog specialize behavior while reusing Animal's implementation.

questions.prompt: Polymorphism means:

options.text: One class can't have many methods
The SAME interface can be used across different underlying types (a variable of type Animal can hold Dog, Cat; calling .speak() dispatches correctly)

questions.explanation: 'Many forms'. Subtype polymorphism (OO) + parametric polymorphism (generics) + ad-hoc (overloading) are the main flavors.

questions.prompt: Abstraction means:

options.text: Exposing WHAT an object does, hiding HOW — via interfaces, abstract classes, or protocols

questions.explanation: Callers depend on an abstract contract, not concrete implementation. Enables substitution + testing.

questions.prompt: 'Composition over inheritance' means:

options.text: Prefer HAS-A relationships (building from smaller parts) over deep IS-A hierarchies to avoid rigid coupling

questions.explanation: Deep inheritance chains cause fragile-base-class problems + hard-to-change hierarchies. Composition = flexibility.

questions.prompt: Java interface vs abstract class — key difference?

options.text: Interfaces: multiple can be implemented, only method signatures (+ Java 8 defaults); abstract class: single inheritance, can have state and non-abstract methods

questions.explanation: Since Java 8 interfaces have default + static methods; since 9 have private methods. But no instance state.

questions.prompt: The SOLID acronym stands for: (select all)
questions.explanation: 5 principles from Robert C. Martin. Deep dive lives in the Software Engineering module.

questions.prompt: Liskov Substitution Principle says:

options.text: Objects of a superclass should be REPLACEABLE with subclass objects without breaking correctness

questions.explanation: Classic violation: `Square extends Rectangle` — setting width shouldn't force height to match, but LSP says a Square used as a Rectangle must still behave right.

questions.prompt: The 'diamond problem' arises when:

options.text: A class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base — ambiguity about which grandparent version to use

questions.explanation: C++ handles it via virtual inheritance; Python via MRO (C3 linearization); Java disallows multiple class inheritance to avoid it (interfaces only).

questions.prompt: Static (class) methods differ from instance methods in that:

options.text: They belong to the class itself, not any instance; called without an instance; can't access instance state

questions.explanation: Utility functions grouped by concept. `Math.max`, `Integer.parseInt` are classic examples.

questions.prompt: In `a && b`, if `a` is falsy, `b` is:
questions.explanation: Short-circuit lets you use `a && a.fn()` as a null guard without extra syntax.

questions.prompt: What does `null || 'default'` return in JS?
questions.explanation: `||` returns the first truthy operand. `??` returns the first non-null/undefined (so `0 ?? 5` → 0 vs `0 || 5` → 5).

questions.prompt: `!(a && b)` is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: De Morgan's Law. `!(a || b) === !a && !b`. Useful when inverting complex conditions to reduce negation.

questions.prompt: FizzBuzz: 1..n. If divisible by 3 → 'Fizz'. By 5 → 'Buzz'. By both → 'FizzBuzz'. Otherwise the number.
Leap year: divisible by 4 AND (not by 100 OR by 400).
questions.explanation:
```js
const isLeap = y => y % 4 === 0 && (y % 100 !== 0 || y % 400 === 0);
```
2000 is leap. 1900 is not. Classic compound-condition test.

questions.prompt: `5 & 3` vs `5 && 3` in most languages:
questions.explanation: Bitwise operates on binary representation. Logical short-circuits and returns the operand value (JS/Python) or a boolean (Java/C#).

questions.prompt:
What does this return when x = 15?
```js
const r = x < 10 ? 'small' : x < 20 ? 'medium' : 'large';
```
questions.explanation: Ternaries chain right-associatively. Fine for 2-3 branches; use if/else or lookup table for more.

questions.prompt: Grade classifier: 90+ = 'A', 80-89 = 'B', 70-79 = 'C', 60-69 = 'D', else 'F'. Handle negative / >100 as 'invalid'.
Given three sides, return 'equilateral' / 'isosceles' / 'scalene' / 'invalid' (a+b>c for all pairs).
In JS, which of these is TRUTHY?
questions.explanation: Falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Non-empty string '0' is truthy — classic gotcha in `if (input)` validation.

questions.prompt: Return true if two date ranges [aStart, aEnd] and [bStart, bEnd] overlap (inclusive).
questions.explanation:
```js
const overlap = (aS, aE, bS, bE) => aS <= bE && bS <= aE;
```
De Morgan reverse of the non-overlap conditions. Classic 'condition puzzle' that trips up candidates who try to enumerate cases.
